246.title: Judaism: hear
246.hook: the central declaration: hear, O Israel, the Lord is one (Deuteronomy 6:4)
246.howItsDone: Observant Jews recite the Shema in the morning and evening prayers and at bedtime, often covering their eyes; its words are written in the mezuzah on the doorpost and in tefillin.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vesak, lanterns and a full moon to close our Buddhist visit. Your line was the full moon. Did you find the moon, and give something away? Day two hundred forty-six, and a new visit: Judaism.

Most faiths have a sentence at their center. For Jews, it's six Hebrew words, and they're said twice a day, morning and night, often with the right hand over the eyes. They're whispered to children at bedtime. They're written on a tiny scroll inside a case on the doorframe of Jewish homes. And for centuries, Jews facing death have tried to make them their last words. What's striking is the very first word. It isn't believe, or pray, or obey. It's listen. Today's word: Shema.
screen: `SIX HEBREW WORDS, TWICE A DAY.` → `ON THE DOORFRAME, AT BEDTIME.` → `SHEMA.`

segments.voice: The words come from the book of Deuteronomy, chapter six, verse four, where Moses speaks to the people before they enter the land. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." In Hebrew, it begins Shema Yisrael. Shema means hear, but it's a rich word: listen, pay attention, understand, take it to heart, even obey. It's hearing that changes what you do. And notice who's addressed. Not one person alone. Israel, the whole people. Then the verse that follows: "And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might." The passage goes on to say these words should be on your heart, taught to your children, spoken when you sit at home and walk on the road, when you lie down and when you rise up, bound on your hand and written on your doorposts. And Jews do exactly that. The Shema is said in the morning and evening prayers. It's written inside the mezuzah on the doorpost and inside tefillin, the small leather boxes some Jews bind on the arm and head for weekday morning prayer. When they say it, many Jews cover their eyes, shutting out everything else to listen. A guest's note: when Jews read the divine name, written in English as LORD, they don't pronounce it, but say Adonai, my Lord, instead. The Talmud tells of Rabbi Akiva, put to death by the Romans, dying with the Shema's last word, one, on his lips. The center of Jewish faith begins with an open ear.
screen: `DEUTERONOMY 6:4.` · `SHEMA: HEAR, HEED, TAKE TO HEART.` · `LIE DOWN, RISE UP, DOORPOSTS.` · `EYES COVERED, TO LISTEN.` · then, large: `HEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen, for the length of the bell. Settle and breathe. If you like, cover your eyes with your hand, the way many Jews do for the Shema. Now just hear. The nearest sound. Then something farther away. The hum of the room. Your own breath. Don't name them or judge them. Just let hearing be the whole practice. The bell holds the time.
Shema. Hebrew for hear, listen, take to heart: the first word of Judaism's central declaration, said morning and night. Today's word.
Your line: hear. Today, in one conversation, listen the way the Shema asks: fully, to take it to heart, not just to wait for your turn. Day two hundred forty-six.

247.title: Judaism: covenant
247.hook: a people bound to God through Abraham, Sinai and the Torah
247.howItsDone: Jews understand their life of Torah and commandments as living within the covenant; brit milah, circumcision on the eighth day, marks a baby boy's entry into the covenant of Abraham, and many communities hold a naming ceremony for girls.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shema, six words that begin with listen. Your line was hear. Did you listen to someone fully, to take it to heart? Day two hundred forty-seven.

Think of the difference between a contract and a marriage. A contract says: if you do this, I'll do that, and if you don't, we're done. A marriage says something stranger: we belong to each other now, through good years and bad, and even when one of us fails, the bond is still there to come back to. Jews have a word for the relationship between God and the Jewish people, and it's much closer to the second than the first. It runs through the whole Hebrew Bible. Today's word: brit.
screen: `A CONTRACT, OR A MARRIAGE?` → `A BOND TO COME BACK TO.` → `BRIT.`

segments.voice: Brit is Hebrew for covenant, a binding promise between two parties. The Torah tells of several. After the flood, God makes a covenant with Noah and every living thing, never again to destroy the earth by flood, and sets a rainbow in the clouds as its sign. Jewish tradition sees that covenant as embracing all humanity. Then Abraham. God promises him descendants as many as the stars and a land for them, and the sign of that covenant is circumcision, brit milah, still performed for Jewish baby boys on the eighth day, which is why many people know the word as bris. Then Sinai, the great one. The people, freed from Egypt, stand at the foot of the mountain. Moses reads them the book of the covenant, and in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation they answer: "All that the LORD hath spoken will we do, and obey." In Hebrew, naaseh venishma: literally, we will do, and we will hear. The rabbis of the Talmud loved that order. Doing before fully understanding, like people in love who say yes before they know every detail. At Sinai the covenant is the Torah itself, the teaching and the commandments, a whole way of life given and received. And Deuteronomy says it was made not only with those standing there that day, but with those not yet there. Many Jews understand that to include every Jewish generation since. The covenant runs two ways: God bound to a people, and a people bound to God. Jews have argued with it, struggled with it and wept over it for thousands of years. They've also kept it.
screen: `NOAH: THE RAINBOW, ALL LIFE.` · `ABRAHAM: STARS, LAND, BRIT MILAH.` · `SINAI: WE WILL DO, AND HEAR.` · `WITH THOSE NOT YET THERE.` · then, large: `A PROMISE KEPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one promise you keep. Settle and breathe. Think of a commitment that's lasted: to a person, a family, a friend, a community, a craft, a faith. Not the ones you broke, just one you've kept. Remember how it began, and a hard stretch when keeping it cost you something. Notice what it's made of you. Let yourself feel the weight of it, and the steadiness. The bell holds the time.
Brit. Hebrew for covenant: the binding bond between God and the Jewish people, through Abraham, Sinai and the Torah. Today's word.
Your line: a promise kept. Today, do one small thing that honors a commitment you've made, without being asked: a call, a visit, a task finished. Day two hundred forty-seven.

248.title: Judaism: study is holy
248.hook: learning is itself worship, and argument is honored (Pirkei Avot 1.1)
248.howItsDone: Many Jews study Torah and Talmud in pairs called chavruta, reading aloud and debating line by line, and a weekly portion of the Torah is read in synagogue through the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday: brit, covenant, a people bound to God by a promise. Your line was a promise kept. Which small promise did you keep? Day two hundred forty-eight.

Picture a room full of long tables. Two people sit across from each other with one big book open between them, and they are arguing. Not whispering. Arguing, out loud, fingers on the page, one shaking her head, the other laughing. Twenty pairs like that, all at once. It's loud enough to sound like a train station. If you walked in without knowing, you'd think something had gone wrong. In a traditional Jewish house of study, this is the sound of something going right. Today on our visit to Judaism: why study itself can be holy, and why the arguing is part of it.
screen: `A ROOM OF LONG TABLES.` → `PAIRS, ARGUING OUT LOUD.` → `THE SOUND OF SOMETHING GOING RIGHT.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Torah. In the narrowest sense it means the five books of Moses, the scroll in the ark of a synagogue. The Hebrew root has to do with teaching, pointing the way, so the word also stretches to mean all Jewish teaching, the whole conversation that grew around the scroll. That conversation has a famous first line. Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, a short book of sayings in the Mishnah, opens by tracing a chain: Moses received Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua, Joshua to the elders, the elders to the prophets, and on to the teachers of the great assembly. Learning, in other words, is something handed from person to person, like a lamp passed down a line. The Torah itself asks for this. In Deuteronomy, right after the Shema we heard two days ago, it says, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children." Teaching the young is not a hobby here; it sits inside the central prayer. Then the surprise. Jewish tradition honors argument. The Talmud records the debates of two ancient schools, the house of Hillel and the house of Shammai, who disagreed again and again. A heavenly voice, the story goes, declared that both were the words of the living God, and the law followed Hillel partly because his students were humble and taught Shammai's view before their own. That's why study often happens in pairs, called chavruta, from the word for friend. You don't learn alone. You push, your partner pushes back, and the text opens.
screen: `TORAH — TEACHING, POINTING THE WAY.` · `A CHAIN FROM SINAI, HAND TO HAND.` · `TEACH THEM DILIGENTLY.` · `BOTH ARE WORDS OF THE LIVING GOD.` · then, large: `LEARN TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's a small practice. Take one line, any line you've met on this path, or the one from today: teach them diligently. Say it once, slowly. Now imagine a partner sitting across from you. What question would they ask about it? Who is them? What does diligently look like on a Tuesday? Let the question sit. You don't need an answer yet. The bell holds the time.
Torah. From a root about teaching and pointing the way: the five books of Moses, and the whole living conversation around them. Today's word.
Your line: learn together. Today, share one line with someone, a friend, a child, a coworker, and ask what they hear in it. Disagree kindly if you like. Day two hundred forty-eight.

249.title: Judaism: repair
249.hook: many Jews speak of repairing the world, a phrase with old mystical and modern meanings
249.howItsDone: Many Jewish communities and families organize acts of service, charity and advocacy under the name tikkun olam; some also connect everyday commandments and blessings to Isaac Luria's idea of lifting sparks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Torah, teaching handed hand to hand, and argued over in pairs. Your line was learn together. Did you share a line with anyone? Day two hundred forty-nine.

Somewhere in your home there's a thing that's been broken for months. A drawer that sticks. A lamp with a loose switch. A shirt missing one button, folded at the bottom of the pile. You walk past it every day. It's too small to matter, and somehow too annoying to fix. Now zoom out. The street has its broken things too. So does the town, and the country, and the whole world, and all of it can feel far too big for one person. Jewish tradition has a phrase that sits right between the button and the world. Today: tikkun olam.
screen: `THE DRAWER THAT STICKS.` → `THE WORLD THAT FEELS TOO BIG.` → `TIKKUN OLAM.`

segments.voice: Tikkun means repair, or setting right. Olam means world. Repairing the world. Today many Jews use the phrase for acts of justice and kindness: feeding people, protecting the vulnerable, caring for the earth. But the phrase has lived at least three lives, and each one is worth knowing. The first life is legal. In the Mishnah, around the year 200, the rabbis made certain adjustments to the law, about divorce documents and freeing captives, and gave their reason as for the repair of the world, meaning to keep society in good working order. The second life is in prayer. The Aleinu, said at the end of Jewish services, hopes for a day when the world will be set right under the kingship of God. The third life is mystical. In the sixteenth century, in the hill town of Safed, the teacher Isaac Luria told a remarkable story. At creation, divine light was poured into vessels too fragile to hold it, and they shattered. Sparks of holiness fell and scattered into everything. Every good deed, every blessing, every commandment kept, lifts a spark back up and helps mend what broke. In the twentieth century, the phrase grew wider again, and many Jewish groups made it a banner for social action. Jews themselves debate how the old and new meanings fit together, and that debate is part of the story. There's also an old saying in Pirkei Avot, from Rabbi Tarfon: it isn't your job to finish the work, but you aren't free to walk away from it either.
screen: `TIKKUN — REPAIR. OLAM — WORLD.` · `FOR THE GOOD ORDER OF THE WORLD.` · `SHATTERED VESSELS, SCATTERED SPARKS.` · `NOT YOURS TO FINISH, NOT YOURS TO QUIT.` · then, large: `REPAIR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: fix one broken thing. First, sit and let one come to mind. The sticking drawer, the loose button, a message you owe someone, a small promise that cracked. Choose one you could mend today. Picture your hands doing it, start to finish. Just one. Not the world, just one spark. The bell holds the time.
Tikkun olam. Repairing the world: a legal phrase, a line of prayer, a mystical picture of gathering sparks, and a call to justice. Today's word.
Your line: repair. Today, fix the one broken thing you picked, and notice how it feels to leave one small corner of the world mended. Day two hundred forty-nine.

250.title: Judaism: blessings
250.hook: a blessing for bread, for thunder, for a rainbow: noticing through words
250.howItsDone: Observant Jews say a bracha before and after eating and at many moments of the day, from waking to seeing lightning or a rainbow, and many aim for a hundred blessings daily.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tikkun olam, repairing the world, one spark at a time. Your line was repair. Did one broken thing get fixed? Day two hundred fifty.

Thunder rolls over the house. Most of us flinch, check the window, maybe check the weather app. Now imagine that your first response, before any of that, was a sentence. A short, fixed sentence that you'd learned for exactly this moment. Another one for the first rainbow after the storm. Another for the first bite of bread. Another for new shoes, or seeing the ocean after a long time away. Your whole day would be stitched with small sentences, each one a way of noticing. In Jewish life, there really is a sentence for all of these. Today: the bracha, the blessing.
screen: `THUNDER OVER THE HOUSE.` → `A SENTENCE FOR THIS MOMENT.` → `THE BRACHA.`

segments.voice: Bracha, blessing, and most blessings begin the same way: baruch atah Adonai, eloheinu melech ha-olam. Blessed are you, Lord our God, ruler of the universe. Then comes the ending that fits the moment. Before bread: who brings forth bread from the earth. That's the blessing called hamotzi. For thunder: whose strength and might fill the world. For a rainbow, a lovely one: who remembers the covenant and keeps the promise, a nod back to Noah, and to brit, the covenant, from a few days ago. Why bless before eating something you already have? The Talmud gives a sharp answer. It quotes a psalm, in the King James words, "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof," and reasons that enjoying anything from the world without a blessing is like taking what isn't yours. The blessing is a kind of asking permission, and a kind of thank-you, at once. There's even a goal. The Talmud records a teaching of Rabbi Meir that a person should say a hundred blessings every day. Between the prayers, the meals and the moments, many observant Jews reach it. Here is the quiet gift in this. A blessing makes you stop and name the thing. You can't bless bread you haven't noticed. You can't bless thunder while scrolling past it. The fixed words do the noticing for you, until noticing becomes a habit. And the first word, baruch, is the root of the name Baruch, and of Benedict in Latin: blessed.
screen: `BLESSED ARE YOU, RULER OF THE UNIVERSE.` · `BREAD, THUNDER, RAINBOW.` · `THE EARTH IS THE LORD'S.` · `A HUNDRED BLESSINGS A DAY.` · then, large: `BLESSED IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless one ordinary thing. Look around and pick something plain. A cup of water. The chair holding you. The light through the window. Look at it properly, as if it were new. If you pray, you can say the traditional opening, blessed are you. If you don't, simply name it slowly: this water, this chair, this light. Let the naming be the thank-you. The bell holds the time.
Bracha. A blessing: a fixed sentence that begins blessed are you, and turns bread, thunder and rainbows into moments noticed. Today's word.
Your line: blessed is. Today, before you eat, pause long enough to name what's in front of you. Two words are enough. Day two hundred fifty.

251.title: Judaism: Shabbat candles
251.hook: on Friday at dusk, two candles are lit and rest begins
251.howItsDone: In many Jewish homes, two candles are lit shortly before sunset on Friday with a blessing, the eyes covered, and Shabbat is kept until nightfall on Saturday; how strictly varies from family to family.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bracha, the blessing, a sentence for bread and thunder. Your line was blessed is. Did you pause and name what was in front of you? Day two hundred fifty-one.

Friday, late afternoon. Think of what the end of a work week usually feels like. The inbox still open. The groceries half put away. The phone buzzing with plans. Now picture a kitchen table in a Jewish home at the same hour. The table is set. Someone strikes a match and lights two candles. She draws her hands around the flames three times, covers her eyes, and says a blessing. When she uncovers them, something has changed. Nothing in the room moved, and yet the week is over. For the next twenty-five hours or so, it's Shabbat. Today: the two candles.
screen: `FRIDAY, THE INBOX STILL OPEN.` → `A MATCH, TWO FLAMES.` → `THE WEEK IS OVER.`

segments.voice: Shabbat means rest, or ceasing. It runs from just before sunset on Friday until nightfall on Saturday. Why two candles? A common answer comes from the two times the Ten Commandments appear in the Torah. In Exodus the commandment begins, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society words, "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." In Deuteronomy the same commandment begins with a different verb: observe it, or guard it. Remember, and keep. One candle for each. In many homes the candles are lit by the woman of the house, though anyone may light them, and the custom is to light a little before sunset, so no one lights a fire once Shabbat has begun. The covering of the eyes has a practical reason: a blessing usually comes before the act, but here the blessing is what begins the rest, so you light, hide the flames, bless, and then look. Now the big idea. For six days, the Torah says, God made the world, and on the seventh God rested. Shabbat invites people to copy that rhythm. No work, no buying and selling, in many homes no phones or driving. Observance varies widely: Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and secular Jews keep it in very different ways. The twentieth-century teacher Abraham Joshua Heschel called Shabbat a palace in time: most holy places are buildings, but this one is built out of hours. And an old saying, from the writer Ahad Ha'am, turns it around: more than the Jews have kept Shabbat, Shabbat has kept the Jews.
screen: `SHABBAT — REST, CEASING.` · `REMEMBER, AND KEEP: TWO CANDLES.` · `LIGHT, COVER, BLESS, LOOK.` · `A PALACE IN TIME.` · then, large: `REST ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, a small version for now. Picture two flames in front of you, or look at any light nearby. Name one thing from this week that you're putting down, just for these two minutes: a worry, a task, a screen. Then name one thing you want to remember. Put down, and remember. If it's near Friday, you might light two real candles at dusk. The bell holds the time.
Judaism, through Shabbat: rest from Friday sunset to Saturday night, begun with two candles for remember and keep. Today's word.
Your line: rest arrives. Today, choose one moment to stop on purpose, a meal without a screen, ten minutes of nothing, and let rest arrive instead of chasing it. Day two hundred fifty-one.

252.title: Passover, the freedom meal
252.hook: each year families retell the going out from Egypt around a table (Exodus 12)
252.howItsDone: Each spring Jewish families hold a Seder on the first night of Passover (the first two nights in many communities outside Israel), reading the Haggadah, eating matzah and bitter herbs, and answering the children's questions.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shabbat, two candles for remember and keep. Your line was rest arrives. Did you stop on purpose, even once? Day two hundred fifty-two, the last day of our visit to Judaism.

A long table, extra chairs borrowed from the neighbors. A plate in the middle with odd things on it: a bone, a roasted egg, bitter herbs, a paste of apples and nuts. Crackers that look like they've been ironed flat. The youngest child at the table stands up, a little nervous, and asks a question everyone has been waiting for: why is this night different from all other nights? And the grown-ups answer with an ancient story, told as if it happened to them. Today, to end our week with Judaism: Pesach, Passover.
screen: `A PLATE OF ODD THINGS.` → `WHY IS THIS NIGHT DIFFERENT?` → `PESACH.`

segments.voice: Exodus tells the story. The Israelites are slaves in Egypt. Moses asks Pharaoh to let them go, plagues fall, and on the last night God passes over the houses of the Israelites, marked with the blood of a lamb. Pesach comes from that verb: to pass over. They leave in such a hurry the bread has no time to rise, which is why the flat bread, matzah, is eaten for the whole festival. And then the Torah does something unusual. It doesn't only tell the story. It commands the retelling. In the King James words: "And thou shalt shew thy son in that day, saying, This is done because of that which the LORD did unto me when I came forth out of Egypt." Unto me. Not unto my ancestors. The Mishnah takes that seriously: in every generation, a person should see themselves as if they personally went out of Egypt. So the Seder, the ordered meal, is built to make you taste it. Bitter herbs for the bitterness of slavery. Salt water for tears. Four cups of wine for freedom. The book at the table, the Haggadah, answers the child's question with a line that is today's carry: we were slaves to Pharaoh in Egypt, and now we are free. Look back at our week. Shema, hear. Brit, a promise kept. Torah, learned together. Tikkun olam, repair. Bracha, blessed is. Shabbat, rest arrives. And Pesach, a people who remember freedom by eating it, together, every year.
screen: `PESACH — TO PASS OVER.` · `NO TIME FOR THE BREAD TO RISE.` · `AS IF YOU WENT OUT YOURSELF.` · `BITTER HERBS, SALT WATER, FOUR CUPS.` · then, large: `WE WERE SLAVES, NOW FREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember one story of freedom. Maybe it's a family story, someone who crossed a border, left a bad job, got sober, walked out of something. Maybe it's your own. Let it come. Now tell it to yourself the Passover way, as if it happened to you, in the present tense. Notice what was bitter. Notice what was sweet. The bell holds the time.
Pesach. Passover: the festival that retells the going out from Egypt around a table, so each generation tastes freedom. Today's word.
Your line: we were slaves, now free. Today, tell one story of freedom to someone else, out loud, the way it's told at the Seder table. Day two hundred fifty-two. Tomorrow we visit Christianity.

myth: the Torah commands the Exodus story to be retold to children
Exodus 13:8: thou shalt shew thy son in that day.
the Seder remembers the Exodus as something that happened only to ancestors
the Mishnah says each generation should see itself as if it went out of Egypt.
Pesach comes from the verb to pass over
God passes over the marked houses on the last night (Exodus 12).

fork.setup: the youngest child asks: why is this night different? how does the table answer?
options: we were slaves in Egypt, and now we are free.
fork.reveal: the Haggadah answers with the story, told in the first person, and the food on the table makes it tasted.

original.note: Hebrew: Passover, from the verb to pass over.

trapdoor: what you thought: a spring holiday with crackers.
what it means: the festival retelling the Exodus, so each generation tastes slavery and freedom.
what a scholar hears: Exodus 12–13, and Mishnah Pesachim 10:5: in every generation one must see oneself as having gone out of Egypt.
